extraction.name: CT-RATE
extraction.description: CT-RATE is a public dataset comprising 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 unique patients, each accompanied by a corresponding radiology report. The dataset includes 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes (over 14.3 million 2D slices) and is annotated with 18 abnormalities. It is designed to support the development of AI foundation models for 3D medical imaging.
extraction.creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, Sezgin Er, Chenyu Wang, Furkan Almas, Ayse Gulnihan Simsek, Sewal Nil Esirgun, Irem Dogan, Omer Faruk Durugol, Benjamin Hou, Suprosanna Shit, Weicheng Dai, Murong Xu, Hadrien Reynaud, Muhammed Furkan Dasdelen, Bastian Wittmann, Tamaz Amiranashvili, Enis Simsar, Mehmet Simsar, Emine Bensu Erdemir, Abdullah Alanbay, Anjany Sekuboyina, Berkan Lafci, Ahmet Kaplan, Zhiyong Lu, Malgorzata Polacin, Bernhard Kainz, Christian Bluethgen, Kayhan Batmanghelich, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Bjoern Menze
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from Istanbul Medipol University, involving chest CT volumes paired with radiology text reports. Data anonymization and annotation were managed by team members, and metadata attributes including patient demographics, scanner parameters, and imaging characteristics were recorded.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Paired chest CT volumes (3D computed tomography scans) and radiology text reports, along with extensive metadata including scanner parameters (manufacturer, tube current, exposure time, convolution kernel, etc.), patient information (sex, age, position), and imaging characteristics (slice location, pixel spacing, reconstruction diameter, etc.).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Manual annotation of 1,000 radiology reports for 18 distinct abnormalities was performed to finetune a pretrained language model (RadBERT) for automated label extraction. Three board-certified radiologists independently rated 150 reports for each model on a scale from 0 to 10 based on predefined clinical criteria, with cases stratified into low, medium, and high clinical accuracy ranges.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned text classifier's precision, recall, and F1 scores were evaluated across 18 abnormalities, showing robust classification. Expert radiologist scores were reported per radiologist for CT-CHAT, RadFM, and CT2Rep.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For expert evaluation of report generation, each of 150 reports was rated by 3 board-certified radiologists independently.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Three board-certified radiologists performed expert evaluation of generated reports.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT, a pretrained language model, was finetuned to automatically extract 18 abnormality labels from radiology reports. Llama 3.1 7B was used to generate over 2.7 million question-answer pairs from CT-RATE reports. A Llama score (LLM-based metric) was used to evaluate clinical accuracy of responses.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset originates from a single institution in a single geographic and clinical setting, which may introduce biases and limit generalizability to other populations.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Limitations include: (1) single-institution data limiting generalizability; (2) CT-CLIP's dependence on specific terminology and prompt choices in reports; (3) lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI benchmarks for comparison; (4) models limited to chest CT volumes only, not extending to MRI, PET, or other anatomical regions; (5) generated report quality insufficient for clinical use.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables development of AI models for 3D medical imaging that could assist radiologists, improve accessibility of medical AI, and support educational and clinical research. However, the models are not yet ready for clinical deployment due to challenges in robustness, interpretability, and regulatory compliance.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes patient age (ranging from 18 to 102 years) and sex information, as well as medical imaging data (chest CT volumes) and corresponding radiology reports.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, validation, and fine-tuning of 3D medical imaging foundation models, including zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, radiology report generation, visual question answering, and downstream clinical tasks such as prognosis and disease grading. Not recommended for direct clinical deployment without further validation.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset, models, multi-abnormality labels, visual question-answering dataset, and a graphical user interface are open-sourced via GitHub. Future work is planned to extend the dataset to other imaging modalities and anatomical regions, but no specific versioning or deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Multi-abnormality labels were extracted from radiology reports using an automated text classifier (finetuned RadBERT) with 1,000 manually annotated reports for 18 abnormalities. Over 2.7 million question-answer pairs were derived from CT-RATE using Llama 3.1 7B for CT-CHAT training. Nodule segmentation information (lobar location, centroid, diameters, volumes) was extracted using a 3D nodule segmentation algorithm and integrated as structured input to CT-CHAT.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: CT volumes were reconstructed using various methods to suit different window settings, resulting in 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes from 25,692 scans. Each exam includes impression and findings sections from radiologist-authored reports. The dataset was divided into training and internal validation sets. Two external validation sets from independent studies in different countries were incorporated. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) were generated from 3D CT volumes for comparison with 2D models.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Within CT-RATE, we manually annotate 1,000 reports for 18 distinct abnormalities for this finetuning procedure... we conducted expert evaluations with three board-certified radiologists who independently rated 150 reports for each model (CT-CHAT, RadFM, and CT2Rep). To ensure a fair and comprehensive assessment, we did not select cases randomly; instead, we used the Llama score on CT-CHAT outputs to stratify cases into low (0–3), medium (4–6), and high (7–10) clinical accuracy ranges, selecting 50 cases from each range. Each radiologist then scored the reports on a scale from 0 to 10 based on predefined clinical criteria.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: The finetuned model's precision, recall, and F1 scores, detailed in Supplementary Table 2, show robust classification across abnormalities, ensuring the CT-RATE dataset is enriched with high-quality labels... The mean expert scores demonstrate CT-CHAT's clear superiority: Radiologist 1 rated CT-CHAT at 3.44 (vs. RadFM 0.55, CT2Rep 2.66); Radiologist 2 at 4.10 (vs. RadFM 0.91, CT2Rep 2.52); and Radiologist 3 at 4.52 (vs. RadFM 0.86, CT2Rep 2.74).

rai:dataBiases.evidence: biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence our self-supervised training. Although we curate a large and diverse set of volume-report pairs, the data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of our models to other populations.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: our CT-RATE dataset and the CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT models have certain limitations. First, biases inherent to our single-institution dataset... Second, CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts... Third, the evaluation of CT-CHAT faces limitations due to the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants... Finally, our current models are limited to chest CT volumes.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: it remains far from ready for clinical deployment, as emphasized by our radiologists. As with all AI systems, challenges such as robustness, interpretability, regulatory compliance, and prospective validation must be addressed before integration into routine radiology workflows.
